extracted.intended_audience: writers, artists, and critics seeking aesthetic/theoretical guidance for fiction and art
extracted.subtask_description: A set of aesthetic principles for producing imaginative literature and art that prioritises style, invention, and artifice over realism or historical/social representation. Intended to guide artists who wish to cultivate 'lying' (beautiful falsehood) as the proper aim of Art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's autonomy (Art never expresses anything but itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art never expresses anything but itself. It has an independent life, just as Thought has, and develops purely on its own lines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat art as self-contained and self-governing: do not assume art's purpose is to represent the spirit, morals, or facts of its age. Example guidance: art is "not necessarily realistic in an age of realism, nor spiritual in an age of faith" and "the only history that it preserves for us is the history of its own progress." Anti-pattern: reading a work primarily as a mirror of its historical moment; scoring a piece by its topical accuracy rather than by its internal aesthetic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject external standards of resemblance (Art as veil, not mirror)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art finds her own perfection within, and not outside of herself. She is not to be judged by any external standard of resemblance. She is a veil, rather than a mirror.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate art by its internal artistic merits — form, invention, style — not by how faithfully it reproduces external reality. Examples: art can create forms ("flowers that no forests know of") that have no real-world counterparts. Anti-pattern: demanding factual accuracy or literal resemblance as primary virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style over factual Truth (Truth is a matter of style)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Truth is entirely and absolutely a matter of style.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise the manner of presentation (tone, diction, imaginative shaping) as the source of a work's truth-value. Use style to generate credibility and emotional/ethical impact ("style makes us believe in a thing—nothing but style"). Example: portraits are more believable when dominated by the artist's style rather than slavish likeness. Anti-pattern: equating verisimilitude with artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: The proper aim of Art is Lying (telling beautiful untrue things)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lying, the telling of beautiful untrue things, is the proper aim of Art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace imaginative invention and deliberate untruth as the core purpose of art — to charm, delight, and give pleasure. Practical cultivation: popular education in conversational circles, literary lunches, and deliberate practice in narrative invention; recognise many forms (lying for art's sake, lying for moral ends, pedagogic lies). Anti-pattern: moralising that treats only factual truth as worthy; suppressing imaginative invention because it is 'untrue.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Realism; translate Life/Nature into artistic conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: “All bad art comes from returning to Life and Nature, and elevating them into ideals... Life and Nature may sometimes be used as part of Art’s rough material, but before they are of any real service to art they must be translated into artistic conventions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use life and nature only as raw material to be transformed into conventions and forms of art; do not simply copy them. Methodological rule: Realism as a method is a failure; the artist must convert observation into aesthetic language. Anti-patterns: literal realism, treating modern life/modernity as the prime subject without transmutation into style or convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid modernity of form and subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “The two things that every artist should avoid are modernity of form and modernity of subject-matter... The only beautiful things are the things that do not concern us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer timeless, non-contemporary subjects or forms (antique, foreign, imaginative) rather than directly depicting the current age. Examples: use older epochs, mythic or exotic material, or invented types. Scoring note: originality that deliberately refuses current fashions rates highly; topicality and immediate reportage rate poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art develops on its own lines; favour formal/medium innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The highest art ... gains more from a new medium or a fresh material than she does from any enthusiasm for art, or from any lofty passion... At other times it entirely anticipates its age.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value innovation in medium, technique, and form as primary drivers of artistic progress; anticipate rather than follow social trends. Example: an artist who invents a new type or mode may be ahead of their age and later be recognised. Anti-pattern: relying on topical passion or social movements as the main source of artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life (and Nature) imitate Art; artists invent social/types to be copied
rubrics_metrics.description: “Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life... The Greeks ... set in the bride’s chamber the statue of Hermes or of Apollo, that she might bear children as lovely as the works of art that she looked at... A great artist invents a type, and Life tries to copy it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and exploit the power of fiction and style to shape real behaviour, taste, and perception. Create convincing types and archetypes: these may become models that society emulates. Examples offered: Balzac’s characters shaping nineteenth-century life; artists shaping fashions, physiognomies, and even climate-perception. Scoring note: assess influence and imaginative force — does the work propose memorable, repeatable types?

rubrics_metrics.name: Use art to create effects that reframe perception of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “External Nature also imitates Art... Things are because we see them, and what we see, and how we see it, depends on the Arts that have influenced us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sensory/evocative effects (mood, atmosphere, image) that alter how readers/viewers perceive everyday phenomena. Examples: painters' invention of fog or light influencing how society perceives climate or sunsets. Anti-pattern: assuming natural description is neutral or purely objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate lying for different purposes but prize lying-for-art’s-sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde distinguishes many forms of lying — for personal advantage, for moral purposes (education), for livelihood, and the highest: lying for its own sake (Lying in Art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate intentions behind invention: pedagogic/moral 'white lies' have social uses; journalistic/political lies serve utility; but the artist should cultivate lying as aesthetic practice above pragmatic motives. Practical suggestions: promote imaginative lying in conversation and education; consider producing a 'When to Lie and How' primer as a tongue-in-cheek method of advocacy. Anti-pattern: condemning all untruths equally and thereby stifling imaginative creation.
